Misconduct Accounts for the Majority of Retracted Scientific Publications
  • Source: PNAS, Vol. 109, No. 42, October 16, 2012
  • Topic: Research misconduct and retractions in biomedical literature
  • Author(s): Ferric C. Fang, R. Grant Steen, Arturo Casadevall
1. Study Overview
  • Database: 2,047 retracted biomedical/life-science articles indexed by PubMed (as of May 3, 2012)
  • Earliest retraction: Published 1973, retracted 1977
  • Key finding: 67.4% of retractions due to misconduct vs. only 21.3% due to error
  • Temporal pattern: Fraud retractions increased ∼10-fold since 1975
1.1 Retraction Categories
  • Fraud or suspected fraud: 43.4%
  • Duplicate publication: 14.2%
  • Plagiarism: 9.8%
  • Error: 21.3%
  • Unknown/other: remaining cases
2. Causes of Retraction
2.1 Data Sources Used
  • PubMed retraction announcements
  • Office of Research Integrity reports
  • Retraction Watch, news media, public records
  • Secondary sources led to reclassification of 118 of 742 (15.9%) retractions from error → fraud
2.2 Example Cases
  • Biochemical and Biophysical Research Communications: Announcement said "methodological flaws" → Harvard investigation found "many instances of data fabrication and falsification"
  • Journal of Cell Biology: Authors said FOXO1a expression findings "not correct" → ORI found first author "knowingly and intentionally falsely reported"
2.3 Retraction Notice Limitations
  • 119 instances: No reason provided for retraction
  • Authors often write their own retraction notices
  • Investigation process averages 20.48 months (up to >9 years)
  • Some journals (e.g., Journal of Biological Chemistry) refuse to explain retractions
3. Temporal Trends
3.1 Timeline of Increases
  • First discernible rise in fraud/error retractions: 1990s
  • Dramatic rise in fraud retractions: Last decade (2000s)
  • Plagiarism/duplicate publication increases: Only since 2005
3.2 Key Triggers
  • Formation of Office of Scientific Integrity (predecessor to ORI): 1989
  • Passage of Whistleblower Protection Act: 1989
3.3 Rate Changes
  • Fraud/suspected fraud as percentage of total articles: ↑ ∼10-fold since 1975
4. Geographic Patterns
4.1 Fraud/Suspected Fraud Origins
  • Top countries: United States, Germany, Japan, China account for three-quarters of fraud retractions
4.2 Plagiarism/Duplicate Publication Origins
  • China and India collectively > United States for plagiarism cases
  • Duplicate publication pattern similar to plagiarism
5. Journal Impact Factor Analysis
5.1 Correlation with Retraction Cause
  • Fraud/suspected fraud: Highly significant correlation (R² = 0.08664, P < 0.0001)
  • Error: Highly significant correlation (R² = 0.1142, P < 0.0001)
  • Plagiarism/duplicate publication: Only slight correlation (R² = 0.01420, P = 0.0243)
5.2 Mean Impact Factor Comparison
  • Fraud/suspected fraud or error: Significantly higher than plagiarism/duplicate publication (P < 0.0001)
5.3 Journals with Most Retractions
Journal Total Retracted Impact Factor
Science 70 32.45
PNAS 69 10.47
Journal of Biological Chemistry 54 5.12
Nature 44 36.24
Anesthesia & Analgesia 40 3.07
6. Time-to-Retraction Data
6.1 By Cause of Retraction
Cause n Mean Months SD
All causes 2,047 32.9 34.2
Fraud (fabrication/falsification) 697 46.8 38.4
Suspected fraud 192 29.4 30.0
Plagiarism 200 26.0 32.6
Duplicate publication 290 27.0 30.1
Error 437 26.0 28.0
6.2 Trends Over Time
  • ↑ Average time-to-retraction for recent years (R² = 0.1236, P = 0.0414)
  • High-impact journals: Slightly shorter time-to-retraction for fraud cases (R² = 0.01441, P = 0.0015)
7. Serial Retractors
7.1 Concentration of Fraud
  • 38 research groups with ≥5 retractions account for 43.9% of fraud/suspected fraud retractions
  • Authors with ≥10 retractions: Nearly all retracted for fraud
  • Example: Naoki Mori laboratory → 1 retraction followed by 30 additional rapid retractions
7.2 Undetected Fraud Duration
  • 12 of Mori's retracted articles had been in literature for ≥5 years before detection
8. Most Cited Retracted Articles
First Author Journal Year Published Year Retracted Times Cited Reason
Wakefield Lancet 1998 2004; 2010 758 Fraud
Reyes Blood 2001 2009 740 Error
Fukuhara Science 2005 2007 686 Error
Nakao Lancet 2003 2009 626 Fraud
Chang Science 2001 2006 512 Error
8.1 Citation Patterns
  • Some retracted articles show rapid, sustained decline after retraction
  • Others continue to be cited (e.g., Fukuhara visfatin article still cited for initial identification despite retraction)
  • Wakefield MMR article: Special case with partial/full retractions, extensive media attention
9. Unexamined Fraud Cases
9.1 Known Unretracted Fraudulent Articles
  • Indo-Mediterranean Diet Heart Study: Lancet and BMJ expressed serious reservations; original articles not retracted
  • Mark Spector (Efraim Racker lab): Data fabrication documented; articles remain in literature
  • R.K. Chandra: Fraud in clinical trials proven; only 1 article retracted despite evidence for others
10. Proposed Solutions
10.1 Policy Recommendations
  • Uniform guidelines for retraction notices
  • Centralized database of scientific misconduct
  • Increased use of checklists by authors and reviewers
  • Improved training in logic, probability, and statistics
10.2 Systemic Reforms Needed
  • Enhanced focus on ethics in scientist training
  • Novel reward systems for science (counter "winner-takes-all" economics)
  • More consistent funding for science
  • Dedicated national agencies (e.g., US Office of Research Integrity) to oversee institutional investigations
11. Study Limitations Acknowledged
  • Only a fraction of fraudulent articles are retracted
  • Other more common sources of unreliability exist in literature
  • Misconduct risks damaging credibility of science
  • Fraud may be a sign of underlying counterproductive incentives

Fig. 1a: Fig. 1. (A) Number of retracted articles for specific causes by year of retraction. (B) Percentage of published articles retracted for fraud or suspected fraud by year of publication.
Fig. 3: Relation of journal-impact factor to retractions for fraud or suspected fraud, error, and plagiarism, or duplicate publication. Journal-impact factor showed a highly significant correlation with the number of retractions for fraud or suspected fraud (A) (n = 889 articles in 324 journals, R² = 0.0864, P < 0.0001) and error (B) (n = 437 articles in 218 journals, R² = 0.1142, P < 0.0001), and a slight correlation with the number of retractions for plagiarism or duplicate publication (C) (n = 490 articles in 357 journals, R² = 0.01420, P = 0.0243). The mean journal-impact factor of articles retracted because of fraud/suspected fraud or error was significantly different from that of papers retracted because of plagiarism or duplicate publication (D) (error bars ± SEM, P < 0.0001).
Fig. 4: (A) Time-to-retraction as a function of year of retraction. R² = 0.1236, P = 0.0414. (B) Time-to-retraction as a function of impact factor. Journal-impact factor correlated inversely with time-to-retraction for articles retracted because of fraud (n = 697, R² = 0.01441, P = 0.0015) but not other causes.
